meta.title: Broto
meta.description: Broto identifies the species from a photo, ranks the likely causes of the problem and gives you a test to confirm it at home. Then it reminds you to water.

hero.title: One photo, and you know what your plant has
hero.lede: Take a picture of the plant. Broto gives you the species, how to care for it and, when something is wrong, the likely causes in order — with a test you can run at home to tell which one it is.
hero.soon: Coming soon to the App Store and Google Play

blocks.label: What we spotted
blocks.body: The lower leaves yellow first and the soil is still damp from the last watering.

blocks.label: What to do
blocks.body: Let the soil dry three fingers deep before watering again, and check the pot has a hole.

blocks.label: What we spotted
blocks.body: Stretched stem and new leaves smaller than the old ones.

blocks.label: What to do
blocks.body: Move it closer to a window, with no sun hitting the leaves directly.

confirms.text: Push a finger three centimetres into the soil. If it comes out damp two days after watering, the problem is too much water — not fungus.
Look at the stem: if it stretched toward the window and the new leaf came out smaller than the old ones, it is short on light — not pests.

care.label: Light
care.note: Near a window, with no direct sun.

care.label: Temperature
care.note: Keep it away from cold draughts.

mock.toxicText: Keep it away from cats and dogs. This does not replace a vet.
mock.reportHint: Tell us and we will fix the analysis.
mock.grow: It grows in long vines. Train it up a stake or let it trail from a shelf. Cut just above a node to make it fuller.
mock.lore: Known as the money plant. In many homes it is a housewarming gift, for its reputation of taking root anywhere.
mock.feedbackHint: Your answer tunes the next analyses.

how.title: Photograph, find out, save

steps.title: Take the photo
steps.text: Frame the whole plant, pot and leaves. One photo only — Broto asks for no angles, no close-ups and nothing else.

steps.title: Find out

steps.title: Save it

tipsItems.title: The whole plant in frame
tipsItems.text: A close-up of one leaf almost never identifies the species.

tipsItems.title: Good light, steady hand
tipsItems.text: A dark or blurred photo is what fails the reading most.

tipsItems.title: One plant per photo
tipsItems.text: With two in frame, the answer may be about the one you did not mean.

plants.title: My plants
plants.summaryDetail: Water, turn the pot and feed

why.title: A yellow leaf never has just one cause
why.first: Watered yesterday and turning yellow means too much water. Two weeks dry and turning yellow means the opposite.
why.second: Same symptom, opposite cause. So Broto never gives one verdict: it ranks the causes and hands you the test that settles it.

reminders.title: A reminder that never becomes spam
reminders.first: One reminder per plant, at the time you pick for each task. It says her name and what she needs today.
reminders.second: Late? It reminds you again. No “tip of the day”, no streak counter.

brotinho.title: For when the doubt sticks around
brotinho.text: It already knows your plants. Just ask, without explaining again which species it is and when you watered it.
brotinho.ask: Can I keep the pothos in the bathroom?
brotinho.answer: You can. It likes the humidity, but it needs indirect light — if the bathroom has no window it will stretch out and drop leaves.
brotinho.subtitle: Answers questions about your plants
brotinho.greeting: Good afternoon. How can I help you?
brotinho.ask2: What about the yellow leaves at the bottom?
brotinho.answer2: The odd bottom leaf going yellow is normal. Several at once usually means too much water — put a finger in the soil before you water again.

items.title: No pesticide dosages
items.text: What you can do without buying anything comes first: prune the affected leaf, adjust watering, improve airflow, isolate it from the plant next to it. If a product is needed, it names the category and tells you to follow the label.

items.title: Never says a plant is edible
items.text: Never, not even if you insist. That is not the kind of mistake you can fix afterwards.

items.title: Never guesses the species
items.text: A close-up of a sick leaf sometimes does not show the plant. When that happens it says it does not know and asks for a photo of the whole plant.

items.title: Never charges for our own failure
items.text: If we cannot read your photo, the credit comes straight back and we say so on screen.

items.title: Does not replace a vet
items.text: The pet-toxicity warning shows up, always with the caveat that it is a warning, not a diagnosis.

items.title: Does not sell your data
items.text: We do not ask for precise location, we do not read your gallery — only the photo you choose to send.

origin.title: It came from a need no app was meeting
paragraphs: Plant apps can tell you the name. You point the camera, Epipremnum aureum shows up, and that is the end of it. But nobody looks at a yellow leaf wanting the Latin name. They want to know what to do.

And there was the other half of the problem: the price. The apps that do more than name the plant charge like professional tools, and they charge the person with three pots on a shelf. That is why Broto starts free and stays useful for free — adding plants, marking that you watered and getting the reminder cost nothing.

The real question is another one: why did this leaf turn yellow? And it has no single answer. It can be too much water, too little water, direct sun, or the plant simply dropping its old leaves. Each one asks something different from you, and doing the wrong one costs the plant.

Broto was born to answer that question. It starts from the photo, names the species because that matters for everything after it, and then goes where the others stop: it lists the likely causes in order, explains what it saw in each one, and gives you a test to run at home, hands in the soil, to find out which one is yours.
origin.quote: A plant cannot talk. But it signals, and that can be learned.

who.title: For people who like plants and will not memorise a manual
who.lede: You do not need to know anything about gardening. You need a plant and a phone.

items.title: It is your first plant
items.text: It came home with a pot and no instructions at all. Broto names the species, says how much water and how much light it needs, and tells you when it is time to do something.

items.title: You have lost plants before
items.text: It is almost always water: too much or too little, and both turn the leaf yellow. Broto tells you which one is yours while there is still time to fix it.

items.title: You have a lot of pots
items.text: Ten, fifteen plants, each on its own rhythm. Broto keeps the routine of every one of them and warns you on the day, so you do not have to remember a thing.

who.note: It works for the plant on the shelf, on the balcony and in the yard — from a succulent to a lemon tree.

items: Tells the cause, not just the name
One reminder per plant, at your time

items.q: Do I have to pay to try it?
items.a: No. The first 3 days have everything the complete plan has, no charge and no card asked. After that you choose whether to subscribe or stay on the free tier.
Analysing a photo needs the internet, because that is what reads the image. Your plant list, the routine and the reminders keep working offline.

items.q: Does it always get the species right?
items.a: No, and it does not pretend otherwise. When the photo is not clear enough, Broto says so instead of inventing a name, and you can correct the species by hand.

items.q: Will it notify me all the time?
items.a: One reminder per plant, at the time you choose for each task. You can switch tasks off one by one, and nothing arrives in the middle of the night.
You can, from the app itself, and the account goes with it. You can also export everything to a file first if you want to keep it.

items.q: Is it for a vegetable garden or a farm?
items.a: It does. It reads any plant you photograph, vegetable beds and fruit trees included, and talks about growing and plant health. Two things it never does: say whether what the plant produces is edible, and give pesticide dosages — there it names the category and tells you to follow the label.
